message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/walls-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/walls-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`, `room_area`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`, `type:beam`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type` (named `Family: Type`), `family-parameter`, `text-type`, `line-style`, `dimension-type`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `normalize_guid`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading, e.g. all rooms of a level), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`), `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator), `slabs::view` (floor, ceiling, roof, shaft, mass; plus `slabs::attached_height(cx, wall_id)` for walls attached to roofs/floors), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs…), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views…), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, floors, roofs, rooms… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/walls-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"room"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: WALLS — `src/readers/walls/` (`walls::view` for wall, room, roomseparator)
Every field `elements` shows for walls, rooms and room separators, exactly, for every kind of project. Observed so far (verify everything):
- wall: the stored fields plus `type` (the type's name instead of its GUID), `type_guid`, `thickness` (the type's), `length` (straight: start–end distance; an arc wall with `"arc": 90` and a 4000 chord shows `length` 4442.882938000001 — unrounded, odd digits: find the exact formula — and `radius` 2828.43, rounded), `room_bounding` (true unless stored false), `height` (the stored one, or worked out to `top_level`+`top_offset`; for walls with `attach_top`/`attach_base` call `crate::readers::slabs::attached_height(cx, id)` — another sub-agent implements it; use its value when Some). Check every location line (`location` stored only when not centre: core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core, interior-core), compound types with layers (`Exterior - 300mm`), flipped walls (`flip` command), `top_offset`, `top_level` null (unconnected), walls by face (`wall_by_face` on a mass), walls on upper levels, walls joined/trimmed (`corner`, `split`), and any other derived field the original adds.
- room: `area_m2`, `perimeter_m` (rounded to hundredths), `enclosed`, `unbounded_height`, `volume_m3` (area × height, rounded), `shares_space_with` (redundant rooms), and whatever else appears (frozen rooms keep a boundary in the file — see what they show). The boundary is worked out at reading time from the room's stored `point`: room-bounding walls on its level that the level's `computation_height` (1200 unless set) cuts, room separation lines (category `roomseparator`, whatever their height), room-bounding columns and structural columns (a 400×400 column inside takes 0.16 m² off and adds 1.6 m of perimeter), free-standing islands (a loop of walls inside a room not joined to its walls) subtracted; measured at the walls' centre lines (`room_area` absent or `centre`) or at their faces (`"room_area": "finish"`: a 4000×6000 centre-line bay between `Exterior - 300mm` walls and a 100 mm interior wall gives 21.66 m² and perimeter 19.0). Unenclosed rooms: area 0, perimeter 0, `enclosed` false (they sit as a 1000 mm square); two rooms in one space: the later one is unbounded, with `shares_space_with` (the other's id). Find the rules for: T-junctions, crossing walls, walls that don't quite meet (gaps, overshoots), overlapping walls, arcs (exact or tessellated? match the digits), walls of different thickness meeting, location lines other than centre (is a centre-line area at the wall's centre or its location line?), room separators crossing walls, columns half inside walls, rotated and round columns, walls whose base/height doesn't reach the computation height (base_offset, low walls, walls from lower levels reaching up), walls with room_bounding false, columns with room_bounding false, `room_area` finish with layered types, rooms on Level 2, `top_level`/`limit_offset`/`base_offset` → `unbounded_height` (2700 = 3000 − 300 to the level above by default; Not Bounded: 2500?), frozen rooms (`frozen` true, `modify {id, frozen}`).
- roomseparator: `length`.
Expose for other readers (I'll wire them later), correct and documented: `pub fn room_loops(cx: &Ctx, room_id: u64) -> Option<Vec<Vec<[f64; 2]>>>` (the room's boundary as the original works it out, outer loop first, then holes; None when unbounded) and `pub fn wall_footprint(cx: &Ctx, wall_id: u64) -> Vec<[f64; 2]>` (its outline in plan, joins applied if you work them out).
Performance: work each level's rooms out once per reading (`cx.cached`); projects can have hundreds of walls and rooms.
Prioritise what typical scripts make (rectangles, L-shapes, subdivided plans with interior walls, T-junctions, separators, columns, finish areas, exterior layered walls, unbounded and redundant rooms) before exotic geometry, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/walls/`.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.

## Performance sample

Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native
file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is
[`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md)
for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC
fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder.

The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you
turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor,
and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor
draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes
transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which.

## Why BIMCraft

- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type
  Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO,
  RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's
  underneath.
- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
...

## What works today

BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:

| Area | Works today |
|---|---|
| Datums | Levels with elevations, each a plane over its extent (a rectangle in plan; by default the model's, a metre past it): sections and elevations draw a level where they see its extent, and the 3D view outlines its plane (its far two edges, all four when selected), hidden behind what's in front, its name lettered on a head past the far edges' right end, a click on either picking it; selected, its ends in a section or an elevation and the middles of its plane's edges in 3D are grips that drag its extent; grids that name themselves 1, 2, 3… or A, B, C… |
| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |

input.description: Read the walls and rooms rows of the table

content.content:
| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

== level ['LL'] Architecture > Level
{elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

== wall ['WA'] Architecture > Wall
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

== wall_by_face ['WB'] None
{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

== room ['RM'] Architecture > Room
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

== room_separator [] None
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

== column ['CL'] Architecture > Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

== structural_column ['CL'] None
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

== flip [] None
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

== modify [] None
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

== corner ['TR'] None
{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

== offset ['OF'] None
{id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved

== trim_extend [] None
{boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several

== split ['SL'] None
{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

== join_polyline ['PJ'] None

content.content:
# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
or ticked in its Visibility/Graphics), every new 3D view so; shown, each is drawn as below, fainter than a selected one,
and a selected room is seen whatever the view says: a see-through solid in the selection's colour from its bottom to its top
(`orbit::room_solid`, drawn over the picture, so it shows through walls). With `room_area {at: "finish"}` (`Model::room_area`, Revit's Area and
Volume Computations) room areas are measured at the walls' faces instead (`face_lines` and the separators), the floor inside them; the IFC space
takes that outline, and its `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities` give both whichever is set: `GrossFloorArea` and `GrossPerimeter` at
the centre lines, `NetFloorArea` and `NetPerimeter` at the faces, `Height` (the room's Unbounded Height) and `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`. Walls, slabs, doors and windows
carry theirs too (`ifc::wall_quantities`): a wall its `Length` on its axis, `Width`, `Height` and side and volume, gross and less the
doors and windows in it (each cut to its height; joins aside), or only `Length` and `Width` when attached, as its height then varies;
a level slab its `Width` (depth), `Perimeter` and area and volume less its openings, a sloped one only its `Width`; a door or window
its `Width`, `Height`, `Perimeter` and `Area`. An attached top or base follows the roof's or floor's plane
over each part of the wall (a roof's slopes each over its own part of the plan); a mirrored wall runs back the other way.
A wall's top is `Model::own_top`, and 3D, sections, plans, IFC and what a wall is attached to all read it there (`walls::heights`
takes it, or what the wall is attached to): its `top_level`'s elevation plus its `top_offset` (file format 15, Revit's Top Offset,
mm, negative below the level), or its base plus its `height` when it has no top level, which an offset does not touch.
`Model::check` refuses a wall whose top does not come out above its base, saying how tall it comes out and by how much to raise it.
The Properties palette shows Top Offset under Top Constraint for a wall that has one.
A roof by footprint is the straight skeleton of its outline and its `courtyards` (`skeleton::faces`: the outline
counter-clockwise, the courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge): each edge moves in at speed 1, a gable's at
0, and its slope rises from it, reaching the roof's base `overhang` in from its eaves; a courtyard's edges number on after
the outline's, and every ring keeps its numbers whichever way round it runs, so `gables` stay put through a mirror.
`Roof::slopes` (file format 15) gives each edge a slope of its own, in degrees, numbered as `gables` are: 0 is the roof's `slope`,
and an empty list, every edge. `Model::roof_faces` then moves an edge in at the run over the rise of its slope, scaled so the
shallowest moves at 1 (every edge at one slope still moves at exactly 1), so edges of different slopes reach the same height
together and the slopes meet along their hips; the eaves stay level, the roof's base `overhang` in from them lowered by the roof's
`slope`, whatever the edges' own. A gable stays upright whatever its slope, and a flat roof (`slope` 0) keeps its `slopes` as it keeps
its `gables`, unused. `Model::check` refuses a list of the wrong length, saying how many edges there are, and a slope outside 0
to 75°, saying which edge. A sketch line may carry a `slope` (`SketchLine::slope`; the Slope row of Properties, with one line of a
roof's sketch picked, sets it): the roof keeps it as the `slopes` of the edges along that line (`sketch::along`), never in its
`sketch`, which `sketch::check` refuses to hold one. `edit_boundary` keeps the slope of an edge that stays or that a new
line cuts in two (an edge lying along an old one), the lines' own `slope` (0 sets the roof's) winning over it, and without
`slope` on the lines it keeps what the edges had; `edit_boundary` without a sketch gives the lines with the slope their edges share.
Over the walls (`floor_outline`, which `roof_footprint` grows by the overhang), a loop of them standing free inside the outer
ones, joined to none of them and with no room in it, is a courtyard, open through the floor and the roof; one joined to them,
or with a room in it, is rooms, and both run over it.
`Model::roof_faces` are its slopes, each the loops round it in plan (a slope can close round a courtyard whose far side is a
gable) with the plane of its underside, trimmed where it `join`s another; `Model::roof_pieces` are those less their holes
and its `openings`, convex where cut. A floor's top is at its level plus `offset`,
or with a slope arrow, there at the arrow's tail and rising `slope` degrees toward its head (`Model::floor_top`); it's its
type's thickness across the slope, so plumb it's thicker. Its `openings` are holes inside it, apart, and `Model::floor_slabs`
what's left, convex where cut. A floor's `shape` (IDEAS MOD-16, [design](../shape-editing.md)) folds its top into planes:
points `z` mm above (negative, below) where the top would be without them, and split lines it folds along, each a part
with an id and a GUID (`ShapePoint`, `SplitLine`). `Model::shape_planes` triangulates its outline, openings, points and
lines (`triangulation::constrained`), lifts each corner by the point there (a corner with none stays at 0) and merges
neighbours in one plane; `Model::floor_faces` are those planes in convex pieces, or the unshaped top, and `floor_slabs`,

neighbours in one plane; `Model::floor_faces` are those planes in convex pieces, or the unshaped top, and `floor_slabs`,
the 3D view, sections and the element's details take them. In IFC a shaped slab is one closed `IfcFacetedBrep`
(`Model::shape_solid`: its top's planes, the same planes under them, plumb sides round its outline and openings, each
corner written once), and a sloped or shaped slab gives `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`, its plan through its depth plumb;
every floor's details give `volume_m3`, what's left of it in plan (shafts too) through that depth. A shaped floor is its type's thickness plumb, so its planes meet
underneath too, and has no slope arrow (`Model::check`, `shape_ok`, refuses one, and points outside the outline or in an
opening, points within a millimetre of each other, a split line's end that is no point and no corner, and lines that
cross). A wall attached to one follows `Model::shape_triangles`, its top over the whole outline as if its openings were
closed, as a slope arrow's plane runs on over them. Plans draw each plane's edges as thin as the outline. `edit_shape`
gives the shape anew or says what it is, `add_point`, `add_split_line` and `reset_shape` change it a piece at a time (an
end of a line that is no point becomes one, at the height the top has there), `edit_boundary` keeps what stays inside the
new outline and its openings, cuts a split line where it leaves them, and gives each new end and each new corner a point at
the height the top had there, so a hole cut through a shaped top leaves it as it was round the hole; it names what it
`dropped`, `cut` and `added`. Moves and mirrors take the shape along, and snaps find its points. A flat roof by
footprint (`slope` 0, no extrusion, joining none) takes a shape too (`Roof::shape`, `Roof::unshapeable` says why another
can't): the commands, checks and both views' tools see its top as a floor's (`Model::shapeable`, `Model::roof_as_floor`:
its footprint, its courtyards and openings as openings, at its top), and `roof_faces` lays each plane's underside its
thickness below, plumb (`roof_rise`), so its slabs, IFC, sections and the walls attached under it follow its falls; plans
draw its creases thin. Under its type's variable layer a shaped roof's underside stays level at its base
(`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`), as a floor's does: its layers in 3D and sections share `Variable::bounds` through
`Model::variable_under`, walls attached under it stop at that underside, IFC writes it as one closed faceted Brep
(`Model::roof_solid`), and `Model::check` refuses a point that leaves the layer thinner than nothing. `falls` (`falls.rs`) gives a floor or a flat roof its shape from its drains and the least fall:
catchments nearest each drain, ridges between them at the top's height, valleys from each drain to its catchment's corners,
each drain as deep as the fall takes its farthest corner; round an opening the valleys turn at its corners, which lie on
the drain's cone, and ridges drawn part the top first. A slab or flat roof whose top isn't one plane comes in from IFC
shaped (`import::shaped_top`), its variable layer marked by its `Description` or, under a level underside, guessed
(`import::guess_variable`); and a spot slope (`Spot::slope`) reads a floor's or roof's fall in a plan. A layer of a floor or roof type may be `variable` (one a type at most; never a wall's or a ceiling's): under a
shaped floor of that type, the underside stays level where the unshaped floor's was (`Model::floor_under`), the layers
above the variable one follow the top, those below it stay level, and the variable one takes up the difference
(`Variable::bounds`, which the 3D view's layers and sections share). Its pieces are then prisms from that level underside
(`Model::floor_prisms`), its volume is less where its top falls (`Model::floor_volume`, `model::volume` for IFC), a wall
attached under it stops at the level underside, and `Model::check` refuses a point that would leave the variable layer
thinner than nothing, saying by how much to raise it. Reinforcement arms a shaped floor only when a variable layer lies
over all its structure: the bars keep to the layers under it, as on a level floor that thick. Without one it refuses,
saying why. In the desktop, a floor selected shows Shape Editing in its contextual tab: Slope Arrow, Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner or an edge's two ends,
`Floor::shape_pick`, to the Options Bar's Elevation), Add Point (a
click on the top, at the Options Bar's Elevation, above the unshaped top or, with Absolute, above the level; empty, the
top's height there), Add Split Line (two clicks, snapping to points, corners and edges) and Reset Shape, each a command.
While one is on, each point's height is labelled beside it (`Model::shape_labels`); under Modify Sub Elements a point's
grip drags it in plan at its height, its split lines with it (`Shape::moved`), in one `edit_shape`. In the 3D view the
same tools work on the floor's top: each point's and corner's grip drags its height up or down, and clicks land on the top
(`view3d::shape_handles`, `on_floor_top`, `shape_pick_3d`); both views run `shape.rs`. While a grip is held, either
view draws the creases its release will leave (`Model::shape_creases` of the floor with the shape it would have). Type Properties ticks a floor's or a roof's variable layer. A ceiling's `offset` is its underside; its `openings` are holes as a floor's

== detail [] None
{view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. Without `detail` it only says what the view has

== inspect [] None
{} levels, element counts, types, warnings and undo history

== render [] None
{family?, type?, mode?: 3d|plan|elevation, wall_thickness?, view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, a sheet's number, or {3D}, ceiling?, width?, height?, path?, azimuth?, elevation?, eye_elevation?} a family on its own with `family` — its `type` (the first by default) standing in a model of its own, in a wall `wall_thickness` mm thick (200) if it's a door's or a window's, nothing of this project's touched or left behind: `3d` (as seen from the south-east), `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on, as seen from the north), a PNG as `pngBase64` or at `path`. Without it: a level's floor plan (with `ceiling`, its reflected ceiling plan, looking up from 2300 mm), a section, an elevation, a sheet (at 5 px a paper mm), or the 3D view seen from `azimuth` degrees round from east (counter-clockwise) and `elevation` degrees up (by default from the south-east, 30° up), fitted; in perspective (see `perspective`) through its lens, and with `eye_elevation` from an eye that high (mm) looking at the same point, as a PNG (pngBase64), or written to a path: .png, .svg for a plan, .pdf for a sheet. A plan, section, elevation or sheet that could not draw something as asked (a fill pattern too dense for the view, more ink behind a region than is kept above it) says so in the reply's `notes`

== graphics [] None
{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)

== section_box [] None
{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

== measure ['ME'] None
{from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing

import math, itertools
# walls: 1 (0,0)->(4000,1000); 4 (-1000,4000)->(0,0); thickness 200 -> h=100 (left face = interior since drawn CCW)
want = (72.76068751089917, 121.26781251816692)
A0=(0.0,0.0); A1=(4000.0,1000.0); B0=(-1000.0,4000.0); B1=(0.0,0.0)
h=100.0
def normals(a0,a1,h):
    dx=a1[0]-a0[0]; dy=a1[1]-a0[1]; L=math.hypot(dx,dy); L2=math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy)
    out={}
    out['n=(-dy/L,dx/L)*h'] = ((-dy/L)*h, (dx/L)*h)
    out['n=(-dy*h/L,dx*h/L)'] = (-dy*h/L, dx*h/L)
    out['n=(-dy,dx)*(h/L)'] = (-dy*(h/L), dx*(h/L))
    out['n=(-dy/L2,dx/L2)*h'] = ((-dy/L2)*h, (dx/L2)*h)
    out['n=(-dy,dx)/L*h'] = (-dy/L*h, dx/L*h)
    out['n=-(dy/L)*h'] = (-(dy/L*h), dx/L*h)
    u=(dx/L,dy/L)
    out['u then n'] = (-u[1]*h, u[0]*h)
    out['u2 then n'] = (-(dy/L2)*h, (dx/L2)*h)
    inv=1.0/L
    out['inv'] = (-dy*inv*h, dx*inv*h)
    out['inv2'] = ((-dy*inv)*h, (dx*inv)*h)
    return out
def lines(a0,a1,n):
    p=(a0[0]+n[0],a0[1]+n[1]); q=(a1[0]+n[0],a1[1]+n[1])
    return p,q
def inters(p1,p2,q1,q2):
    out={}
    d=(p2[0]-p1[0],p2[1]-p1[1]); e=(q2[0]-q1[0],q2[1]-q1[1])
    den=d[0]*e[1]-d[1]*e[0]
    t=((q1[0]-p1[0])*e[1]-(q1[1]-p1[1])*e[0])/den
    out['p+t d']=(p1[0]+t*d[0],p1[1]+t*d[1])
    s=((q1[0]-p1[0])*d[1]-(q1[1]-p1[1])*d[0])/den
    out['q+s e']=(q1[0]+s*e[0],q1[1]+s*e[1])
    # cramer line eq
    a1_=p2[1]-p1[1]; b1_=p1[0]-p2[0]; c1=a1_*p1[0]+b1_*p1[1]
    a2_=q2[1]-q1[1]; b2_=q1[0]-q2[0]; c2=a2_*q1[0]+b2_*q1[1]
    det=a1_*b2_-a2_*b1_
    out['cramer']=((b2_*c1-b1_*c2)/det,(a1_*c2-a2_*c1)/det)
    # p + d * t with t computed via cross(q1 - p1, e) / cross(d, e) with other order
    t2=((q1[0]-p1[0])*e[1]-(q1[1]-p1[1])*e[0])/(d[0]*e[1]-d[1]*e[0])
    out['p+d*t2']=(p1[0]+d[0]*t2,p1[1]+d[1]*t2)
    # lerp form
    out['lerp']=(p1[0]*(1-t)+p2[0]*t, p1[1]*(1-t)+p2[1]*t)
    out['lerp2']=(p1[0]+(p2[0]-p1[0])*t, p1[1]+(p2[1]-p1[1])*t)
    out['lerp_s']=(q1[0]*(1-s)+q2[0]*s, q1[1]*(1-s)+q2[1]*s)
    # determinant form (wikipedia)
    x1,y1=p1;x2,y2=p2;x3,y3=q1;x4,y4=q2
    D=(x1-x2)*(y3-y4)-(y1-y2)*(x3-x4)
    out['wiki']=(((x1*y2-y1*x2)*(x3-x4)-(x1-x2)*(x3*y4-y3*x4))/D, ((x1*y2-y1*x2)*(y3-y4)-(y1-y2)*(x3*y4-y3*x4))/D)
    return out
NA=normals(A0,A1,h); NB=normals(B0,B1,h)
for (kn,na) in NA.items():
    nb=NB[kn]
    pa=lines(A0,A1,na); pb=lines(B0,B1,nb)
    for order in [0,1]:
        if order==0: r=inters(pa[0],pa[1],pb[0],pb[1])
        else: r=inters(pb[0],pb[1],pa[0],pa[1])
        for k,v in r.items():
            mark = '<<<<' if v==want else ('x' if v[0]==want[0] else ('y' if v[1]==want[1] else ''))
            if mark: print(kn, order, k, v, mark)
# unit direction based lines
print('done')

    cmds += ['--cmd', 'rotate {"ids":[%d],"about":[0,%d],"angle":%s}' % (100002+i, i*10, a)]
